areas.name: Which platforms and stores the game must reach

areas.name: Install, trust, and updates
areas.brief: Decided: the app updates itself; signing comes later on both systems; the Mac app ships unsigned with steps to allow it; saves stay in today’s folder. Core: all three. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Stay in the browser, but make it feel like an app
areas.brief: Decided: a browser app window or an installable web app is off the list. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A thin shell on the system web view (Tauri and similar)
areas.brief: Decided: lean to Tauri 2. Core: lean Tauri. Open: confirm Tauri with a trial against the three proofs. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A shell that ships its own browser (Electron and similar)
areas.brief: Decided: Electron is the fallback, with one browser and one test tool, but a large download and no touch. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A game engine as the host (Unity, Godot)
areas.brief: Decided: Unity, Godot, and Bevy are off the list; 3D is a wish. Scope: kept.

areas.name: How the engine and the page talk inside a package
areas.brief: Decided: one engine interface with two paths. Core: two paths and the same stream on both. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Testing and iteration speed
areas.brief: Decided: the full suite inside the app on every system. Core: the full suite and the three proofs. Open: the macOS build needs a Mac and an Apple account. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A crash inside the app
areas.brief: Decided: direct calls stay, and engine errors are caught at the boundary with a restart from the last stoppage. Core. Risk: a hard crash still closes the app. Scope: kept.

areas.name: One match per start
areas.brief: Decided: playing again without a restart waits for the season layer. Core. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Builds and test runs on three systems
areas.brief: Decided: local builds for Windows and Linux now, hosted CI later; the first trial proves Windows and Linux, and the Mac proof comes later. Core. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Replay files open the app
areas.brief: Decided: the app registers the replay file type. Core. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A native Rust interface with no web page (GPUI and its community fork)
areas.brief: Decided: Tauri stays the lean; a GPUI pitch probe runs beside the Tauri trial, against a bar of a smoother pitch and a working test story; the web page rule can change if it passes. Open: the GPUI base, picked by a licence audit. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Unreal Engine as the host
areas.brief: Core: the probe shape (Unreal only, a 2D pitch, one dense native screen, an in-process bridge passing the same byte stream). Scope: mixed.

items.text: The installed game starts the engine, serves the page, and opens it in the player's default browser; each start plays one match.
The page reaches the engine over a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1, and the engine serves the page itself with cross-origin isolation headers.
The Windows setup file is about 2.6 MB and is not signed, so SmartScreen warns before it runs.
The product constraints say plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, MIT- or Apache-compatible dependencies only, and Windows 11 first as a browser page served by a local engine process.
Installers and packaging for other operating systems were deferred as a named later piece of work in the match engine workflow.
The existing HTML page stays the user interface, whatever the package is.
A Unity host pulls against the rule of permissive-licence dependencies only, and Unity does not render HTML without a separate web view plugin.
The browser chrome makes the game feel like a website.
A closed tab or a browser crash ends the match while the engine keeps running.
The default browser can be any browser at any version.
The tab is tolerable; the push comes from stores, trust, and other platforms.
The game must be able to ship on Steam.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: The game must run on macOS and Linux desktops as well as Windows.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: A tablet or phone is a real future target.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: A touch target later pulls against shells that build for desktops only, such as Electron.
Reach to stores and platforms drives the package choice, not the pains of the browser tab.
items.why: Chosen as the top pain; the tab itself is tolerable.

items.text: Steam is a wish for someday, not a plan.
items.why: Chosen for Steam timing.
items.accepted-risk: A package chosen without Steam in mind can mean a second package when Steam comes.

items.text: Touch does not shape the package choice now; repackage when touch comes.
items.why: Touch is far enough away.
items.accepted-risk: A desktop-only shell means a second shell when touch comes.

items.text: All four readings hold at once: a Mac and Linux build, trust and install, one choice that grows to Steam and touch, and a richer view later.
The browser-tab release already ships for Linux, and a Mac build needs Apple signing and notarization whichever shell is chosen.
Unity came up for a 3D match view someday.
Unity came up because most games use it.
Unity came up to rule it in or out.
The product names the Football Manager 3D view as an anti-reference, because cluttered overlays hide the play.
A 3D view can live in the page itself with WebGL and a permissive library, with no game engine host.
The next release delivers one app window that can later grow to Steam and touch, before a Mac build, a signed install, or a richer view.
items.why: Chosen as the one thing the next release delivers.
items.accepted-risk: The next release adds repackaging work with no new player feature, and the unsigned-setup warning stays.

items.text: A 3D view is a someday wish and does not weigh on the package now.
items.why: Chosen for what 3D means for the game.

items.text: Unity stays a full candidate beside the web shells.
items.why: Chosen for the Unity verdict.
items.accepted-risk: With 3D only a wish, Unity keeps its costs (a licence exception to the product rules and a rebuilt interface or a web view plugin) without its main reason.

items.text: The comparison list is Tauri 2, Electron, Godot or Bevy, and Unity.
items.why: Chosen from the kinds of host.

items.text: A chromeless browser app window or an installable web app is off the list.
items.why: Not chosen; it has no store path.

items.text: Inside the package, the page calls the engine directly in the same program instead of over the local socket.
items.why: Chosen for the engine link.
items.accepted-risk: The page transport is rewritten and tied to one shell, and the browser test suite and replay viewing, which run over the socket today, need their own path.

items.text: The browser test suite drives the page against a live engine it starts, over the local socket.
Direct engine calls in the shell pull against the browser suite and replay viewing, which need the socket path.
A direct call means something different in each host: a Rust command in Tauri, a Node native addon in Electron, a native plugin in Unity, and a rewrite of the page in Godot or Bevy.
The person asked how the choices affect the ability to test and iterate easily, in answer to the summary check.
The official Tauri WebDriver runs on Windows and Linux only; macOS needs WebdriverIO with an embedded plugin or a paid driver.
Our Playwright suite can drive the page in a Tauri window on Windows through the WebView2 debugging port.
Tauri ships mocks for its engine calls, so page unit tests can run with no app window.
Tauri development mode reloads the page on a change and rebuilds the Rust side on a change.
Playwright drives Electron apps directly, but that support is still marked experimental.
An Electron installer is usually about 50 to 150 MB.
A Tauri app on Windows can be under 1 MB, plus about 1.8 MB when the WebView2 bootstrapper is embedded.
Tauri uses a different web engine on each system (WebView2, WKWebView, WebKitGTK), so the page needs testing on all three.
The Steam overlay does not draw over WebView2; a Tauri plugin adds a surface for the overlay as a workaround.
The Steam overlay works in Electron with extra flags and a steady repaint; Vampire Survivors first shipped on Electron.
The main Unity plugin that shows HTML (Vuplex 3D WebView) is paid per platform and has no Linux build.
Unity Personal is free up to 200,000 dollars of revenue; the runtime fee is cancelled; the runtime stays proprietary.
Rebuilding the page in Godot, Bevy, or Unity loses the Playwright suite and the page unit tests, because no browser automation reaches an engine-drawn interface.
A permissive Godot plugin shows a system web view on desktops only; mobile is only planned.
Unity with its HTML plugin pulls against the Linux target, because the plugin has no Linux build.
Direct engine calls only pull against keeping the page tests, which need the page to run in a plain browser over the socket.
One transport interface with two paths: direct engine calls in the app window, and the socket in a plain browser for tests, development, and replays.
items.why: Most page tests survive only if the page still runs in a plain browser over the socket.
items.accepted-risk: Two transport paths must stay equal, and a bug can live in one path only.

items.text: The whole browser suite also runs inside the packaged app on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
items.why: Chosen for app tests.
items.accepted-risk: With Tauri this needs a second test tool on Linux and macOS, and it gives the slowest test runs.

items.text: Unity, Godot, and Bevy leave the list; the comparison is Tauri 2 against Electron.
items.why: The Unity HTML plugin has no Linux build, and a rebuilt page loses every page test.

items.text: The full suite in the app on every system favours Electron, while size, touch later, and a Rust-native engine link favour Tauri.
The choice leans to Tauri 2 over Electron.
items.why: Installer size, a path to touch, and direct calls into the Rust engine with no Node addon.
items.accepted-risk: A second test tool on Linux and macOS, web engine differences between systems, and a workaround for the Steam overlay.

items.text: The first trial or release must show a full match playing in the app window on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
items.accepted-risk: The macOS part needs a Mac to build on and an Apple developer account, which the project does not have yet.

items.text: At least one full browser-suite test must pass inside the app on each system.
One match must give the same event stream over direct calls and over the socket.
A Windows installer near today size was not chosen as a proof.
Is Tauri 2 confirmed as the shell, and does a trial against the three proofs settle it?
The match engine workflow has a finished distribution piece that built the NSIS setup file and the Linux archive; an app shell changes it.
The finished distribution piece of the match engine workflow needs an update for the app shell.
The app checks for a new version and installs it itself.
items.why: Chosen for updates.
items.accepted-risk: A host for update files and an update signing key that must stay safe; a lost key strands every installed copy on its version.

items.text: Code signing comes later on both Windows and macOS, when the game has players.
items.why: Chosen for signing.
items.accepted-risk: Windows keeps the SmartScreen and antivirus warnings, and on macOS most players cannot open an unsigned app without a trip to the system settings.

items.text: The app keeps saves in today’s data folder, so old matches carry over.
items.why: Chosen for saves.

items.text: A full match on macOS as a proof pulls against signing later, because an unsigned Mac app is blocked for most players.
The Mac app ships to players unsigned, with steps to allow it in the system settings.
items.why: Chosen to resolve the Mac proof against signing later.
items.accepted-risk: Most Mac players give up at the block, so the Mac release reaches few players until it is signed.

items.text: The page today shows an engine crash and restarts the engine from the last stoppage with the same score and clock; that works because the engine is a separate process.
The repository has no CI configuration; builds and test runs happen on the owner machine and in WSL.
Direct engine calls in the same program pull against crash recovery, which needs the engine in a separate process.
Direct calls stay; engine errors are caught at the boundary and the match restarts from the last stoppage.
items.why: Chosen for a crash inside the app.
items.accepted-risk: A hard crash, for example running out of memory, still closes the app window.

items.text: Playing the next match without a restart waits for the season layer.
items.why: The season layer changes what the next match is anyway.
items.accepted-risk: Until then, the app plays one match per start and feels like a one-shot launcher.

items.text: Hosted CI comes later; Windows and Linux build locally now, and the Mac waits.
items.why: Chosen for builds.
items.accepted-risk: The Mac proof and the full suite on macOS wait with it.

items.text: The app registers the replay file type, so a double-click on a replay opens it in the app.
items.why: Chosen for replays.

items.text: A season layer design document exists in the realism programme.
CI later with no Mac pulls against the core proofs on all three systems.
The first trial proves the app on Windows and Linux; the macOS proof and the macOS suite runs come with CI or a Mac.
items.why: Windows and Linux can prove the shell now, and there is no Mac and no CI.
items.accepted-risk: Web engine differences on a Mac show up late.

items.text: A GPUI interface pulls against keeping the HTML page and its tests, the same reason Godot and Bevy left the list.
The official gpui crate (Apache-2.0) was last published in October 2025 and is pre-1.0 with frequent breaking changes; current code comes from git or weekly snapshot crates.
An open report says the main GPUI code pulls GPL-3.0 crates through its tracing crates; a relicensed snapshot of that code is not confirmed as legitimate.
The community fork gpui-ce exists so the framework has its own releases apart from the editor; it is Apache-2.0 or MIT, active in 2026, and has yanked and renumbered releases.
GPUI Kit (formerly gpui-component, Apache-2.0) offers more than 75 components and runs a commercial trading desktop app.
GPUI does not render HTML; its only web view crate is experimental, covers Windows and macOS only, and draws over the window.
GPUI tests are Rust tests with simulated input; screenshot tests run on macOS only, and outside automation needs an accessibility change that is not merged.
GPUI runs on Windows, Linux (X11 and Wayland), and macOS; mobile support is experimental and partly GPL or AGPL, and web support is basic.
No shipped game is built on GPUI; the known apps are tools, such as a trading desktop app.
GPUI on Windows needs a DirectX 11 GPU, and a release build needs a compiler from the Windows SDK.
GPUI would fit only if the interface is rebuilt natively in Rust, for very dense live panels with the engine in the same program.
The page is about 5,300 lines of JavaScript, 1,600 lines of CSS, and 290 lines of HTML, with 23 unit test files (about 2,200 lines) and 6 browser suite files (about 1,200 lines).
The socket, recovery, pending-change, and decode code on the page plus the protocol crate come to about 2,700 lines, which a single-program interface would mostly not need.
GPUI draws you for one Rust codebase with no transport, and for the speed and feel of a native GPU-drawn interface.
The one engine interface with two paths can take a third client later, so a native GPUI interface can come after Tauri without undoing it.
A small probe rebuilds only the pitch view in GPUI against the engine interface, to measure the feel and the work before any larger choice.
GPUI can be learned first on a developer tool, for example a calibration dashboard, where a rewrite loses no player tests.
A small GPUI probe rebuilds only the pitch view against the engine interface, beside the Tauri trial.
items.why: To measure the feel and the work of a native interface on a small piece.
items.accepted-risk: A second trial runs at the same time as the Tauri trial and splits the attention of one owner.

items.text: The rule that the interface is plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript can change if the probe shows GPUI is clearly better.
items.why: Chosen for how firm the web page rule is.

items.text: GPUI counts as clearly better only if its pitch runs smoother than the web pitch on the same machine and match, and its pitch tests run on Windows and Linux with a way to drive it from outside.
items.why: Chosen as the bar for the probe.

items.text: The GPUI probe is one more part of the app-shell workflow, next to the Tauri trial, and both end at the same go or no-go.
items.why: Chosen for where the probe lives.

items.text: Which GPUI base does the probe use, gpui-ce or the snapshots with GPUI Kit? A licence audit picks it, because the product rule allows permissive licences only.
Unreal Engine is worth weighing as the package for the game.
Unreal ships a Web Browser widget on the Chromium Embedded Framework, but on an old Chromium: about 90 up to Unreal 5.5, and 128 only from 5.7.

Unreal takes a 5 percent royalty above 1 million dollars gross per game, 3.5 percent when the game launches on the Epic Games Store at the same time, and Epic store revenue is excluded; the source is on GitHub under the proprietary Epic licence.

A Rust library built with a C interface and loaded by a small Unreal C++ plugin works, with several examples; the Linux build fights the Unreal clang and libc++ toolchain, and Windows must match the Unreal C runtime.
An Unreal host pulls against the product rule of MIT-compatible or Apache-2.0-compatible dependencies only.
The reasons that took Unity, Godot, and Bevy off the list apply to Unreal unless Unreal answers them.
The product rules allow MIT-compatible or Apache-2.0-compatible dependencies only.
A rich 3D match view draws you to Unreal.
items.why: Chosen as a reason to weigh Unreal.

items.text: Reach to Steam and to consoles draws you to Unreal.
items.why: Chosen as a reason to weigh Unreal.

items.text: One engine for the long run, so the game does not move a second time, draws you to Unreal.
items.why: Chosen as a reason to weigh Unreal.

items.text: Does Unreal carry today's page in its browser widget, draw a 3D pitch beside the page, or replace the whole interface?
The pull to a 3D view and to consoles pulls against the earlier decisions that 3D is a someday wish and that Steam is someday.
The reasons for Unreal rank in this order: one engine for the long run, then the 3D match view, then Steam and consoles.
items.why: Chosen as the order of the reasons.

items.text: The licence rule gains an exception for a proprietary engine host; code dependencies stay MIT-compatible or Apache-2.0-compatible.
items.why: Chosen so that an engine host such as Unreal can ship.
items.accepted-risk: Unity comes back into the comparison, a royalty applies above 1 million dollars gross, and the product rules and the open-source promise of the project change.

items.text: An Unreal probe takes the place of the GPUI pitch probe beside the Tauri trial, and both end at the same go or no-go.
items.why: GPUI and Unreal both test a move away from the web page, so one probe answers the long-run question.

items.text: In three years Touchline is a 3D match-day game: a broadcast-style 3D view with animated players, and the screens serve the match.
items.why: Chosen as what one engine for the long run means.
items.accepted-risk: The product rules name the Football Manager 3D view as an anti-reference and set a flat, light pitch, so the product identity changes, not only the package.

items.text: The probe uses Unreal only; Godot and Unity are not built.
items.why: Chosen to test the engine that draws you.
items.accepted-risk: The go or no-go compares Unreal only with Tauri, so a lighter engine such as Godot is never measured.

items.text: The Unreal probe draws one live match in 3D from the engine event stream, and today's page runs in the Unreal browser widget for one screen.
items.why: It answers whether the 3D match works and how the screens live beside it.

items.text: Unreal wins the go or no-go only if one real page screen works in its browser widget and sends a change the engine applies, and a test drives that screen and checks the 3D pitch from outside.
items.why: Chosen as the must-pass checks for the probe.
items.accepted-risk: The bar does not require a live match through the C++ bridge or a Linux build, so Unreal can win while the bridge and the Linux target are still unproven.

items.text: In packaged Unreal 5.6 Linux builds, the browser widget cannot load a local file or a localhost page, and Epic has not answered the report.
The page in the widget can call the game through window.ue, and the game can run page JavaScript, but only through a small C++ subclass of the widget.
An empty Unreal 5 shipping build for Windows is about 320 MB, trimmed to about half, and the browser plugin adds about 150 MB; today the setup file is about 2.6 MB.
No confirmed way exists to attach Playwright to the browser widget in a packaged Unreal game; it likely needs a change to the plugin, or a move to the Unreal Automation and Gauntlet tests.
No public evidence shows the browser widget on PlayStation, Xbox, or Switch, and Chromium does not target consoles, so the web page screens likely cannot ship on a console.

The game code, the Rust crate, and the page can stay public under MIT or Apache-2.0, and builds can ship, but any engine change cannot be public and every contributor must accept the Epic licence to build.
The page inside the Unreal widget pulls against consoles as a reason for Unreal, because the widget likely cannot run on a console.
The bar that a test must reach the widget screen pulls against the finding that no confirmed way exists to attach Playwright inside a packaged Unreal game.
The Unreal probe rebuilds one real screen with Unreal's own interface tools; that screen sends a change the engine applies, and no browser widget is used.
items.why: The browser widget fails local pages on packaged Linux builds and likely cannot run on a console.
items.accepted-risk: On the Unreal path the web page and its browser suite are replaced by Unreal screens, so a later full move to Unreal rebuilds every screen.

items.text: Unreal wins the go or no-go only if the native screen sends a change the engine applies, and Unreal Automation or Gauntlet tests drive that screen and check the 3D pitch in a packaged build.
items.why: No confirmed way lets Playwright reach inside a packaged Unreal game.
items.accepted-risk: The browser suite covers the page in the Tauri app only, the Unreal side needs a second test stack, and a go still says nothing about Linux.

items.text: The event stream may not carry enough timing, facing, ball flight, and contact detail for believable 3D animation, so the 3D view may invent movement that contradicts the match.
items.evidence: consult codex, session 3 (the oracle could not read the files; built from the prompt context)

items.text: A 3D engine leaves two possible owners of the ball, player positions, and contact; the Rust engine must stay the owner, or the design changes.
items.evidence: consult codex, session 3 (the oracle could not read the files; built from the prompt context)

items.text: One simple Unreal screen does not predict the cost of the dense manager screens: sortable tables, text entry, keyboard use, and scaling.
items.evidence: consult codex, session 3 (the oracle could not read the files; built from the prompt context)

items.text: The Tauri trial tests packaging today's game, and the Unreal probe tests a future 3D rewrite, so one go or no-go mixes two questions with different bars.
items.evidence: consult codex, session 3 (the oracle could not read the files; built from the prompt context)

items.text: Unreal tests prove little unless they drive the packaged game through the real Rust bridge and compare the result with a known engine run.
items.evidence: consult codex, session 3 (the oracle could not read the files; built from the prompt context)

items.text: The Unreal bar adds a full live match in the packaged probe through the real Rust bridge, with a tactics change, a pause, and a second match after the first.
items.why: The bridge is the part most likely to change the answer.
items.accepted-risk: The probe takes longer, and a go still says nothing about Linux.

items.text: The native Unreal screen in the probe is a dense one, for example the squad list with sorting, selection, and keyboard use.
items.why: It shows the real cost of moving every screen to Unreal.

items.text: Test Unreal with a 2D match pitch.
The Unreal probe draws today's flat 2D pitch, not a 3D one, beside the dense native screen; 3D comes later on the same engine.
items.why: It tests the bridge, the dense screen, and Unreal as the one engine with no 3D art work.
items.accepted-risk: The probe does not test the 3D look, which is the second reason for Unreal.

items.text: The Unreal probe runs first; if Unreal wins, the Tauri release is skipped and the game moves straight to Unreal, and the next release waits for the probe.
items.why: Chosen as how the decision works.
items.accepted-risk: The next release waits for the probe with no player-facing change, and if Unreal wins, the game carries a large engine, a C++ bridge, and rebuilt screens before any player sees an app window.

items.text: Unreal first with the Tauri release waiting pulls against the earlier decision that the next release delivers one app window.
The engine stream is JSON control messages plus small binary position frames (a 99-byte keyframe and a 48-byte delta), with 9 message kinds to the client and 6 JSON commands back.
A C++ client for the stream needs roughly 600 to 900 lines: about 80 for the binary frames, most of the rest for the nested JSON messages.
The engine allows one viewer per match, and each engine process plays one match.

An in-process bridge (Rust built as a C library inside Unreal) takes about 8 to 15 days for the probe: a new C API over the engine, Windows and Linux toolchain fights, and a Rust panic takes Unreal down, losing the crash restart; the Rust-in-Unreal crates are proofs of concept or unmaintained.

An out-of-process bridge, where Unreal starts the unchanged engine and reads its existing socket, takes about 5 to 8 days: a C++ decoder, starting and stopping the engine process, and shipping a second program; no Rust enters the Unreal build and the crash restart keeps working.

Consoles likely do not allow a game to start a second program, so the socket bridge is for PCs only; a later console build can carry the same byte stream through an in-process library and keep the C++ decoder.
items.evidence: platform documentation is under NDA; not confirmed

items.text: Avoid the cost of an in-process bridge by having Unreal read the engine's existing socket.
The Unreal probe links the Rust engine into Unreal as a C library, in-process.
items.why: It is the bridge consoles would need, proven now.
items.accepted-risk: About 8 to 15 days of bridge work in place of 5 to 8, the toolchain fights on Windows and Linux come first, and a Rust crash takes Unreal down unless the crash restart is rebuilt inside Unreal.

items.text: The Unreal bar adds a replay check: Unreal must read recorded matches exactly as the web page does, byte for byte.
items.why: It catches reader bugs early for about a day of work.

items.text: An in-process bridge pulls against the crash restart from the last stoppage, which today relies on a separate engine process.
In the Unreal probe, engine errors are caught at the C boundary, and the match restarts from the last stoppage inside Unreal, as in the Tauri app.
items.why: Chosen to match the Tauri app.
items.accepted-risk: A hard crash, such as running out of memory, still closes the game, and the probe grows.

items.text: The in-process bridge offers new direct function calls to Unreal, such as get players or queue a change, not the existing byte stream.
items.why: Closer to how Unreal code usually works.
items.accepted-risk: A second interface must stay in step with the socket, and the replay check needs its own adapter.

items.text: New direct calls for Unreal pull against the decision that one match gives the same event stream on every path, and against the byte-for-byte replay check.
The in-process bridge hands Unreal the existing byte stream and takes the existing commands; Unreal reads it with a C++ reader of about 600 to 900 lines.
items.why: The same-stream rule then holds on every path with no exception, and the replay check works as is.

items.text: The Unreal probe keeps its full size, roughly four to six weeks for one owner.
items.why: Chosen over shipping Tauri meanwhile or cutting the probe.
items.accepted-risk: The estimate is rough, and the probe competes with the Tauri release for one owner's time.

items.text: The Tauri app window ships as the next release; if Unreal wins later, the Tauri app is a stepping stone.
items.why: The one-app-window release stands over Unreal first.

items.text: The Unreal probe starts after the Tauri app release ships.
items.why: The release comes soonest, and one owner does one thing at a time.
items.accepted-risk: The answer on Unreal waits about four to six weeks after the release.

items.text: The Unreal probe is its own workflow, started after the Tauri release; the app-shell workflow drops the GPUI probe and ends at the release.
items.why: Chosen when the Unreal area closed.

items.text: Rewriting the product rules now pulls against the long-run 3D goal being left for later, because the 3D anti-reference would change before the 3D goal is decided.
The kept probe parts add up to about 24 to 38 days, which overruns the four to six week budget at its upper end.
